source.title: Batch-wise Convergent Pre-training: Step-by-Step Learning Inspired by Child Language Development
source.authors: Ko Yoshida; Daiki Shiono; Kai Sato; Toko Miura; Momoka Furuhashi; Jun Suzuki

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports downstream task scores for two model sizes, providing a limited comparison relevant to V6, but does not measure pretraining-loss scaling or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: Table 2 reports downstream benchmark results for the proposed 115M and 372M models; these are recorded as the study’s direct comparison across sizes. Other tables report training-method, curriculum, and optimizer ablations rather than a clean size comparison, so their scores are not included as evidence about the scaling trend. The paper does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy values, scaling-law fits, or compute-optimal allocations.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a batch-wise constrained pre-training method for BabyLM and reports only that method's downstream scores. Kaplan et al. is cited only in the introduction. Table 2 compares two sizes (115M, 372M), but each is the best configuration chosen by average score. The sizes also differ in depth, width and heads. No loss, scaling fit or size trend is measured or claimed, so this two-point comparison of the authors' own method cannot test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6) or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude the method underperforms the official baselines, especially on grammar tasks such as BLiMP and BLiMP-S. It gives small gains on morphology and discourse tasks such as WUG-ADJ and Entity Tracking, and only incremental gains over controlled baselines. They draw no conclusion about scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains BabyLM models with batch-wise constrained optimization and evaluates downstream benchmark performance; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurement or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported downstream scores vary by task across the two model sizes; the larger model improves on some scores, declines on others, and ties on GLUE. Table 2 reports the best-performing configuration for each size, with both using (p, C) = (1, 10−6).

fits_no_version.finding: Going from 115M to 372M, the paper's selected configurations change average BabyLM score from 32.8 to 33.1, with mixed per-task directions. The Random controlled baseline goes from 31.6 to 33.9 (Tables 3–4). All runs use about 1.18B training tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the BabyLM data-limited regime, tripling parameters at fixed data gives small, task-inconsistent downstream changes.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the First BabyLM Workshop
record.problems: Only two model sizes are compared, with no reported uncertainty or held-out pretraining loss measurements. Model architecture dimensions vary with size, and the reported Table 2 configurations are selected as best-performing across tasks.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 3–5 and 9 contain downstream task scores for training-method, curriculum, and optimizer ablations. They are not extracted because those comparisons address the ablated training choices rather than a clean size-scaling comparison; see Tables 3–5 and 9.

untested.parts: No held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No other modality or regime scaling.
No downstream scaling trend or loss-to-downstream prediction; only two selected configurations of a novel method.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 labels are dropped. The study does not test scaling; it only reports its own method at two sizes, with configurations chosen by best average score. R13's value was copied from the GPT-BERT row. Model sizes differ in several architecture dimensions (Table 6), and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is measured.
The two model sizes differ in multiple architectural dimensions; the paper does not compare architectures at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is tested for a power-law loss form.
The paper compares downstream scores at only two sizes; it does not test prediction from pretraining loss or fit a downstream scaling relationship.
No scaling exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or compared across setups.
